weaknesses: The central comparison is inadequate. The only well-described head-to-head baseline is an independently trained RGB Tri-Plane. There are no competitive multi-scene, category-level, amortized, shared-backbone, learned-initialization, or low-rank/compressed representation baselines. Consequently, the claim of being the most efficient approach to scaled inverse graphics is not established.

The broad resource comparison in Table 4 is not sufficiently documented: training protocols, convergence criteria, tuning, and how each number was measured or extrapolated are absent. Its PSNR values also differ materially from Table 1 without explanation. Comparing methods at unmatched quality further weakens the claimed Pareto advantage.

“Training time” is not accompanied by GPU-hours, utilization, or throughput under controlled parallelism. Independently fitted scenes are trivially parallelizable, while the proposed method jointly batches scenes. Likewise, the reported “memory footprint” is primarily stored representation size rather than peak training memory. These ambiguities directly affect the main efficiency claim.

Evaluation is narrow: two highly aligned, category-specific datasets at only 128×128 resolution, with resource measurements mainly reported for ShapeNet Cars. Results on heterogeneous categories, real complex scenes, higher resolutions, or varying capture conditions are needed to demonstrate that the shared bases scale beyond this favorable setting.

Novel-view metrics are computed for only 50 sampled scenes, with no repeated runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or seeds. Quality differences are mixed: on Cars the method slightly improves PSNR but worsens SSIM and LPIPS, while on faces it improves PSNR and LPIPS but noticeably worsens SSIM. Thus “comparable quality” is plausible but not rigorously substantiated.

The Micro–Macro construction is essentially a learned linear dictionary of shared Tri-Planes concatenated with local features. Its novelty appears modest, and the related-work discussion does not adequately position it against the extensive literature on multi-scene/category-level radiance fields, shared representations, dictionary factorization, or meta-learned scene fitting.

Important sensitivity and scaling evidence is missing, including variation of the 500-scene pretraining set, the local/global feature split, dictionary size beyond M=1 versus M=50, latent resolution, and scene-distribution diversity. Figure 5 appears to plot a linear cost model rather than measured scaling at multiple dataset sizes.

Stage two fine-tunes the shared bases and decoder using only the second subset, which can change representations of first-stage scenes. The paper does not clearly report pre/post-stage-two retention or sequential-addition experiments, leaving the claim that further scenes can be continually added without harming existing ones unsupported.

There are several reproducibility and correctness ambiguities: code is only promised for future release; Equation 6 uses Eψ instead of Eϕ; Equations 8–9 omit shared parameters that the text says are optimized; and multiple inconsistencies or typos occur, including “ShapeNet Cats” for Cars and 9.61 versus 9.71 ms decoding time.
